Specialization, Music Composition (BM Music), Effective Winter 2025 Appendix D Music composition lessons are a bit different than other lessons, and the work typically done in MUS 411 is already done in the lessons.
MUS 411 is enrichment through repertoire, therefore MUS 411 is superfluous for composition students, considering they already engage in rigorous score analysis as part of their composition curriculum.

Composition students typically undergo a curriculum that already includes regular analysis of scores relevant to their lessons, in addition to taking Counterpoint, Form and A nalysis, and Orchestration.
This means they are already exposed to a variety of Western Music styles, techniques, and structures through their coursework.
Composition lessons often involve in -depth discussions and analyses of specific compositional techniques, styles, and works.
These discussions are tailored to the individual needs and interests of the composition students, providing a more targeted and personalized learning experience.
Students not only listen and analyze scores but also actively apply what they learn to their own compositions.
This hands -on approach allows them to directly experiment with techniques and styles discussed in their lessons, r einforcing their understanding and skills development.
Composition students integrate the techniques learned from studying scores (Saariaho, Boulez, Webern, Harvey, Risset, Grisey, Ravel, Berio, Ligeti, Higdon, Aberdam, Revueltas) and sometimes innovate upon these techniques in their own compositions.
MUS 411 is definitely redundant for composition students.

Adjustments have been made to MUS 235, 311 and 312 DUE to a change in credits for music courses, MUS 235 from 2 to 3 credits, and MUS 311 and 312 from 1 to 2 credits.
The result is an additional 2 credits in required courses (MUS 235, and MUS 311 OR 312).
To balance the loss of 4 credits from 411, students will have the opportunity to take 7 cr. of electives instead of 5.

Music composition lessons are a bit different than other lessons, and the work typically done in MUS 411 is already done in the lessons.

Students not only listen and analyze scores but also actively apply what they learn to their own compositions.

This hands-on approach allows them to directly experiment with techniques and styles discussed in their lessons, reinforcing their understanding and skills development.
Composition students integrate the techniques learned from studying scores (Saariaho, Boulez, Webern, Harvey, Risset, Grisey, Ravel, Berio, Ligeti, Higdon, Aberdam, Revueltas) and sometimes innovate upon these techniques in their own compositions.
MUS 411 is definitely redundant for composition students.
